title: A $2.5trn AI shakeout, a US jobs surprise and central banks turning hawkish
dek: Tech leadership cracked, the Bank of England hiked, euro inflation hit 4% and Korea's market had its worst week in years — while oil had its biggest weekly slump since 2020.

mood.label: Nervous
mood.explanation: The VIX — the options market's gauge of expected S&P 500 swings — sat at 23.42 on 9 November, up about 11% on the week and 54% on the month, while CNN's Fear & Greed index was at 25, or "extreme fear", versus 44 a month ago. High-yield credit spreads widened to 3.48 percentage points on 5 November from 3.32 a day earlier, and Reddit chatter was overwhelmingly concentrated in chip and AI-linked tickers rather than broad index funds — attention, not calm.

regions.headline: Jobs beat revives hike talk as tech leads stocks lower
regions.summary: The US economy added 165,000 jobs in October and unemployment slipped to 4.1%, prompting some Fed policymakers to discuss a rate rise rather than a cut. The S&P 500 fell 2.68% on the week to Friday's close and the Nasdaq 3.37%, with an AI-driven selloff wiping a reported $2.5 trillion from market values at its worst. Democrats flipped control of Congress in the midterms.

regions.headline: Euro inflation at 4%, Bank of England hikes to 4%
regions.summary: Euro area inflation reached 4% in October, a three-year high, hardening expectations of an ECB rate rise in December from the current 2.5% deposit rate. The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4%, its first increase since 2023, and warned inflation will approach 5%. European indices still rose on the week, with the IBEX up 3.75%.

regions.headline: Korea and Japan slump, India and Hong Kong rally
regions.summary: The KOSPI fell 14.34% over the week and the Nikkei 7.13% as the global AI selloff hit chip-heavy markets. China reported consumer inflation of 0.7% in October while factory-gate prices rose 5.7%, the fastest in over four years. India's Sensex gained 7.15%, helped by a cheaper oil bill and a firmer rupee.

body:
## Opening

Two things broke at once this week. The trade that has carried global equities for two years — anything connected to artificial intelligence — went into reverse, with [a reported $2.5 trillion wiped from market values](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMidEFVX3lxTFBRNUYxQ2c5VUJvNkd2RExjdVJ1YU5UNmpYYzh2dzgzT2FOZFFaNmlpd0ZUSVViTzZkRG91RmRad3MxNXdncmt4aFFuR2U5di11dmlYSG9hODllU2RNZXFTUHR1UlhpYzhESlpfMS15OVdETTNP?oc=5) before a partial bounce. And the direction of central bank travel flipped: the Bank of England [raised rates for the first time since 2023](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMisAFBVV95cUxQMUY3RVZDLURQel9mZWtEbWI5aEp6eEEyTU50ck5TOHhTenFuSUhVaGlxX0Z1UHF4cUxxeE1tdTZpMjEzaVlaaUQ2TENfVHVYVndJNWFLclNVemtIaEF0RFBWcE55anJ2cnJYT29jWEk5aHJId2NFOFdvNFBPcTZYTnV4UjhmdHotdm1ITmFNWEt5MVltUjlmOThrbWJXdjU0WEhsWllZRE5aam5WX0w2dQ?oc=5), euro area inflation [hit 4%](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiigFBVV95cUxPZE40ZWZuWllSbGhUMVRQLVVNaU5lc1NVWnhZZFFRQWRDbTN1aDllekVocUlJTmZWUi1adGNVdFI5dVlGQ0xNWW9HZGVpanlqVjA2VWxlMFF2elgwWUd6T09hbHhaMTBRRlZzc1RwRVd0Tkc1Q1loZDVkYXpqTkYwY1F1dGxTYzlhZkE?oc=5), and after a punchy US jobs report [some Fed policymakers began talking about a hike](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMimwFBVV95cUxQMF93ekZ4N2wtdW4zX1llS2FoZWpNVlhMLTRNOGVJTUktZmpLQUNBSzY2bW16Mm9mb3lrZERqNFZ6WkRmYkhBTG00Z2k2NFYyNTVLcmVBSkV5eVJRU1RwZFc5blM4MkRmcUxYU2hadXRWbVh0VXpjektqM1BGS3ZlZlNMeW43VWxmeE5TQm13d0E3bTVwUnp5dzFFNA?oc=5). Add a Democratic sweep of Congress in the US midterms and the [biggest weekly slide in oil since 2020](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiuwFBVV95cUxPdnhrZGtNcWxGbkFFblBPWHdiUVRGQ2JLakh6YmF2WC1xX1BOdVlrMGxhakdlZEdRa2ZfV1pmS2pDZzFoaDdVTXBkRVVYWHU0NG9RdENJOWVXTk5vcFR5RFRVRG1HTnZGdHdTM0Y3cGhDY3pVcUFsTXhtQ01kbndfdHBrZnNLTGlXVk41cGlzQ3JiVExNNTBNYjRfNkJRWjhTc2Z6RWM5RU5KTWNGTk1yMjFObWlUMkhoalQw?oc=5), and you have a week in which almost every assumption got re-tested.

## United States

October payrolls came in at [165,000 jobs, well above expectations, with unemployment slipping to 4.1%](https://news.google.?oc=5) from 4.2% in September. That is good news for households in work, but it lands awkwardly: September CPI inflation was 4.02% year on year, up from 3.71% in August, even as core inflation (which strips out food and energy) was steadier at 2.79%. With the fed funds rate at 3.88% in October, [Reuters reported policymakers weighing a rate rise](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMimwFBVV95cUxQMF93ekZ4N2wtdW4zX1llS2FoZWpNVlhMLTRNOGVJTUktZmpLQUNBSzY2bW16Mm9mb3lrZERqNFZ6WkRmYkhBTG00Z2k2NFYyNTVLcmVBSkV5eVJRU1RwZFc5blM4MkRmcUxYU2hadXRWbVh0VXpjektqM1BGS3ZlZlNMeW43VWxmeE5TQm13d0E3bTVwUnp5dzFFNA?oc=5), and commentary pointed the same way — Yahoo Finance called the report [a new reason to hike](https://news.google.?oc=5).

Markets took it badly where it hurt most. The S&P 500 closed Friday at 7,376.86, down 2.68% on the week and 5.51% over the month; the Nasdaq Composite fell 3.37% and is down 9.79% in a month. Bonds were the odd one out: the 10-year Treasury yield was 4.85% on Monday, a little lower than a week earlier, and the gap between 10-year and 2-year yields — the "yield curve", a rough market signal on growth and rate expectations — narrowed to 0.35 percentage points on 6 November. For households, the 30-year mortgage averaged 7.18% on 5 November, barely moved from 7.24% the week before. Borrowing costs are not coming down.

## Euro area

Euro area inflation reached [4% in October, the first time in three years](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiigFBVV95cUxPZE40ZWZuWllSbGhUMVRQLVVNaU5lc1NVWnhZZFFRQWRDbTN1aDllekVocUlJTmZWUi1adGNVdFI5dVlGQ0xNWW9HZGVpanlqVjA2VWxlMFF2elgwWUd6T09hbHhaMTBRRlZzc1RwRVd0Tkc1Q1loZDVkYXpqTkYwY1F1dGxTYzlhZkE?oc=5), with [a December ECB hike now widely expected](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMijwFBVV95cUxNSnlWVjhZeXhCME9sTHdmcC1RWTdrNUVIbUhhbE1td2t3Z2VDbzh1SW1kSmJJdWU5aVRSeW8tQ3hweVJwTDdVMGR0XzdtM0UtSGhkRnY1NWN6ZUkxR05xb2NadnJuNjEza3d4cDNOcTRnWXJBT2MzYnJjY2hkbjdHUmxoWjVsWGE0UE5NOUx0QQ?oc=5) from a deposit rate that has sat at 2.5%. The ECB's own wage tracker pointed to [slightly higher wage growth in the first three quarters of 2027](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiiAFBVV95cUxQOHFzR3BOV3dub2V1MG9uZ0NZTThPcVYwM1NrM3J6Vjdoa3VUUnUzLWM3MVVxZF9FVTEtUF9abTdZZHhURmlhMUlqM19COGNYYzRQTGpBajR3SWxNOVdSY1ZiQ2VsQ0JHX0VuX2Rxek4tQmlROUh4UmRLaDNRa1VWYnRLRXVEMUFY?oc=5) than this year, which will not soothe hawks. For euro area employers, the message is that the cheap-money phase is over: the deposit rate is the floor under corporate borrowing costs, and government bond yields have been drifting up, with France's 10-year at 4.48% in September against Germany's 3.47%.

Britain moved first. The Bank of England [lifted Bank Rate to 4%, unanimously, and said more may come](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMisAFBVV95cUxQMUY3RVZDLURQel9mZWtEbWI5aEp6eEEyTU50ck5TOHhTenFuSUhVaGlxX0Z1UHF4cUxxeE1tdTZpMjEzaVlaaUQ2TENfVHVYVndJNWFLclNVemtIaEF0RFBWcE55anJ2cnJYT29jWEk5aHJId2NFOFdvNFBPcTZYTnV4UjhmdHotdm1ITmFNWEt5MVltUjlmOThrbWJXdjU0WEhsWllZRE5aam5WX0w2dQ?oc=5), while [warning inflation will near 5%](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiswFBVV95cUxNYWs5QVQtM2FoOGZNTEI4Nm55VUVpdGJhQmdXcG5zc3VJWG5aQTU3X2NPT2xIdmdYZW0zdG5VakdqamlqY0VReDI3TzFHcUZBZlU3VU9nLXpzWEI4N0dtcWNueFNSUDFCbzFJcUNvOHdtVEoxUEMweU4tNUNLcWprWG5BRkxWWWNNZ1pfR09XaThGTV9lYXJfLThMdFZBaWFRUms2UjBncExjUjdqMzhXT3Iwcw?oc=5). Mortgage holders rolling off fixed deals and firms with floating-rate debt will feel that directly. Oddly, European equities had a decent week — the IBEX 35 rose 3.75%, the CAC 40 1.96%, the Euro Stoxx 50 1.23% — largely because they carry far less AI exposure than Wall Street or Seoul. The FTSE 100 was flat, down 0.08%. The euro ended at $1.12.

## Asia

Asia bore the brunt of the tech unwind. South Korea's KOSPI fell 14.34% over the week, with [an 8% plunge that triggered a circuit breaker as chip shares tumbled](https://news.google.?oc=5); [Reuters linked the slide to US midterm results feeding an AI selloff](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMixgFBVV95cUxQUXFPZWJ0ekg2Mnl6b3ZEMDRpRzJON3M1b3FnWlpsbVZSSlpnMDR1YXJFWG0zMmROd0NybFRLWXdtcjdQWm1hckFsTE15d2FoY0hnMGZsMjctbnc1VjFCZ09uUWhDbVpGOUtmQmU4UEhLNmtINHZjbTA4cXZPSmpqTFM3TEptUUU4clROU0xCc3QtM3NNbThZOHMxU1lqU1I4Y3EzRnRnY1hqUFpwUTJWcWcxQWhJNVh2VER2dGtzZUxxSmJSeXc?oc=5). Japan's Nikkei 225 lost 7.13%, and [Taiwan, Korea and Japan were all hit hard](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMipgFBVV95cUxOTm5vQzNBZnVpSUdPZWwzU3J2Yi04Y3JXaWpwYjNGVEt2U1lDMjZubjdnQTdKRENVeE94QlhSblNGR0Z6cHl4QjJyVU8tbThXazVnTjVxZ1JfU25YTXlDU3hlNGdQek90TDBGM0V5NWFENFJyM3QyalVDZzd6TzdLcmhHVHpHMzZldGtuck1XMjI5WXNWS1dXWnFZSXJHSmlZbmUzYlpB?oc=5). The contrast elsewhere was stark: Hong Kong's Hang Seng rose 4.51% and India's Sensex 7.15%, with [the rupee rallying on cheaper oil and the midterm outcome](https://news.google.?oc=5).

China's price data told two stories. Consumer inflation [eased to 0.7% year on year in October, below the 0.8% expected](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMitAFBVV95cUxOYkViVnVINnotYUc2cTJqbEhkQ01LYktFY2U4Y1hSd19GZy13QkdzQXJqYWg1S050dFYwa3h3cUJDczd1NGFqdkFFN2xJa1BWV3JGOGxGMl8zb2ttZVJNUmJrVW91LTJSY0twQUYzRWF2UmoxMnV1c3NGek9BejgySW5aZG1JUUlMMDJtVlA1Q1VSQWREdVV5RVZlbkZGX0ZYOXVLUXZTaC0yQXpCVGxjb3BZbGM?oc=5), while [factory-gate prices rose 5.7%, the fastest in more than four years](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMitAFBVV95cUxQMmtVSmRjR3dJWkJYWi1ROURuRTNuVXFmUFBDelZtUkFHQ0pwaWRmVzFJNXhiMEFoS0g0Mmx3UTJoTFpEcWFDVm4tNTZMSmV5NkhrRGs1SWhYMC1iNmpaMG92UlRweV9wTldzNHFLdE1qbUh1U0ltcWdNcDUwVHpaVkhidDlobUM3RTNGV0pIbkR2OUF3akRtamtaRi1iN3VuZXl5VkJlS1IzclV3ZFZNVWhyS2U?oc=5). Weak consumer prices with rising producer prices squeezes Chinese manufacturers' margins and, eventually, nudges up the cost of imported goods elsewhere. In Japan, the finance ministry disclosed that it [spent a record ¥7.9 trillion in a single day on 30 July to support the yen](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiVEFVX3lxTE5FOE1JYzFnTi01ZFdENUg5eWRMNWNEcDdrVG1GUjhGZTgyVmFYcTNtQ0puWjRESmt3Qm9lRnQ0YS1Cc1J4YU1jRzlyTTdQVVBwYmFndg?oc=5) — and yet the yen still sits at 157.9 to the dollar, which [underscores how hard reversing a weak currency is](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMivwFBVV95cUxOVzZJWDNjU0Z5RjdaQlk0Yy1fTlY0VzhPdlRCZTB3aS1IeVFFenJ6TzVTbDJpemdOSDFxSy1jRHNhVzVqY3Q3eUI4M01kdGZqMVJhYVpJcFhreWtpcV94QVkzczRjeGpkZHBKdzJSUWxhRFYzYWo3RVREQjNqU0s5ZERMdEJiRkZ5UWhqY2hlSkdmcUIySGFRUC1CRVd1VzV3R3ZqM2xrZTRTRVZwRG4xNlVIS3d0ODhLUks3Wko4aw?oc=5).

## Debt and politics

Democrats [flipped control of Congress](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMihgFBVV95cUxNQ0ktb3JQam9saVhrUDhjbXZWTDVQaV9tVGFyX0VWdnh1Y3lTd3BDYlBlTFN3WS1tN0szdm4zb184WkZEcnhDZWVaS3h1RHp3azFaUEFfTWNtSjY4UXhXTG5ESjBvRmRHTzluZks0VlBrS1RzR1ZuNVJSa0s3eFNVU3J2WmZpQQ?oc=5), and markets initially cheered — the Dow had [its best post-midterm day in 44 years](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMieEFVX3lxTE5vQVR4WDhsdUVseFU4eUgwa2c4aDRnWFFYV2p3X2o0OEJNbnEwUzl4dXdxd05rZHFXckg5TXB3X3YtX3pLbkxSUWJYdUlpb1NRSlhoRmMyMXd0WUJnNTN0c0hfS3M3SUI3dDJjT2N3VGpxXzdMdGctaQ?oc=5) — before the mood soured as investors reassessed policy exposure, from [AI and crypto trades](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMirwFBVV95cUxPdTRQb3pkNzdfSm5LVl9yeno5dERXdGZNZklXZmpZQUp6SXFNUkZScHpwVElhOHczVkZILWpjWjVMRmVlSlZwa1BjVmxRVzJMSl9neWNxMFNFc0pEMUxoRmd3dmQzcXhEZVliTFlPbElVSHJKTlRiSDhqTkMzcUJuR1l4eE15MEJDMjRfYzlBSWdwZWhDbGVCOEdlNmpJbHBMd0VJTWxJa3BBNUNrUzkw?oc=5) to [data-centre stocks, with renewables rallying](https://news.google.?oc=5). Notably, voters [rejected data-centre ballot measures almost everywhere they appeared](https://news.google.?oc=5), a local-politics constraint on the AI buildout that businesses planning power-hungry projects should note. US federal debt stood at 121.19% of GDP in Q2 2026; euro area government debt was 88.8% of GDP in the same quarter.

Geopolitics was busy. Oil fell hard — Brent down 9.86% on the week to $94.44, WTI down 9.24% — as [Trump signalled restraint on Iran despite fresh shipping attacks](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiqAFBVV95cUxNWnV4VENDNkFNVllVVEpoVTJLcC13SlhHREstWFZZQ252QTRiU3dKeW5EYWYxVUJjNnQzVzh1M1FsWjNGTmRKMVFEYjhxT3M2VmF4aVpERWwwczh6dV9OTG5NcFJCMFVZZ0toWEEyMnRRTnBZUm9iQVVzblIzcmJMOTR4V29sUDFVME1jcFQ5VVhoMHVUM0YzWHM2bmE1b3VCV0s0R2JmUUQ?oc=5) and [attention turned to Iran talks](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMitwFBVV95cUxQMFl0ckZ4NThYdTZVTzJ0NFhySExJLV9famdEQVItUUJFd0Z0eVNhLTNDTHdMUndYUFMtT2lRcWc0dEVEbjlyQ2o0N1ctREpUWmwyT3RIX2lka2tXaU05QUlzdDVFZjdSZUZVTkNlZVNTX0l5U3p6dUVlMUYtaWIxcEtZcGJ3RGNJdUZFT3hKSFdPbjJWaUUwS3JjT3NNS0h0WU1YU2l2bDBlU29VMXBtNDFzSXQ2elE?oc=5), though Washington's top diplomat [saw little hope of a breakthrough](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMibkFVX3lxTE5jUnFoaUY5Uk04NjQzYzVvZzIxYTVvbUhGZTMzSGFFUjdYcVc1ZS1lT3JqUi1rU3pZT1EyNUl2MkZHdFF2cGhzenBldXZJcEpBOXRJUEpjVGVpNUkzWUMtTklXLTNRT01pUmV6ajVR?oc=5). A [Saudi Aramco tower in Riyadh's finance district was targeted in a rare strike](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMitgFBVV95cUxOLUpUaXJBZU5CYXNqcDJjZkEtUlc5MWZRcVlsWmFWaWhDcHRJMTNLM05iV25SMEtHTGZyTTZHN3NlaGlGY1dwUFUxQmxXcFNxdmt5R3J1MVJGbmdjblFVMmR0UldtU2M3b0htSGE0YmNBSnNpd1JtVnJHTWlMMnRycHdYUFR1WGN5ck1rdjM0ZmtjNEstR1ZjZjh5X1d2M3g4RUY0bXVoR1VOOUNuWllTVm9qVzJuQQ?oc=5). [Ukraine peace talks resume in Abu Dhabi](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMihgFBVV95cUxQOE9NUS1DRlJBNF9FaU1BcU5LNjFfX2I2eHRaRkYwOXdLWmdyLU5aUjdLeVJ1WV9nTUQtYVhXNkFfTjQ5dk5hdzJneTJxS0FmNHZKODR0cHpiUTVBanU5S0JGbk5ZTXBjaWNXWGFXN2hRRy13UGZEUWZkUGR4SEl6ODduQXNjQQ?oc=5), with [Europe pressing the US on Ukraine and Iran at G7 talks in Paris](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMilgFBVV95cUxQVUtkODBnQ3Z2TnlSMjlHd3BpZnlEZXRyREVmU3l3RWhLY2ZteGs2cl9UZl9QV3h0eENENVMtRWFoYkFEYmM2V0JPeS00aUh0SWhSaUxPQ2tqSXNfTlhteHhpUjNTRGZzTUdIdWFyU3Ftby1JY1haa3BVNVNrLVRIaWVHenhtdzFJMjNSV05qVnJmQXNDeXc?oc=5). Elections produced [no clear winner in New Zealand](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMivwFBVV95cUxOY3o2eFZkekpBRXNYdktqb2JoT2N5MklUYS1KakpENWdUWUxqaWpSMVRXM3NodXA1aG1JY3JTbDBfTHhleUd4aV9Rd1NiMTJFNmtnRjBYWkpJLUthMGN5aGk3Sk1lanNHY2Fwc2Q2THlvZ0hlbTBxdTVxTEVNa0NaLUEtTVR3cHNZQmhBS0hSTTNnaU1pUkE2QXU5dFUzbHB5bjZhZ1Jha0dXX0JPY3VQbTdTZEJVY3RwcExyczJ5NA?oc=5) and [a setback for the ANC in South Africa](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMirwFBVV95cUxNMUtYd2NsUTR2OTBHcVdmZkd2OWFmYjFIUVRfTGhhcHcwLVc5b2o2bHFob1JxWGhZY2hVelE1c3REN3hULThUMGxpMGZjMXBhMVlmMXJHcmRnVUtBZ3BOZmxJYS0wQ1Y5cGoyaXloell6aWlvLXBGZzZ2U2JuaG50M2VEdU5MdnJjYU5SaWRJT1dCdm1tdS1uak9JWFFNSWFPUVByakJhLWY2T1RKU2ZN?oc=5).

## AI and technology

The AI complex is now the market's main macro variable. [The Guardian asked openly whether the bubble is bursting](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMirgFBVV95cUxPUk5KWGFRY0lPalplQWNSaFZZTk11VEJvblJNWXBnTGlQU05xZTBoVlFzTHprWHVfaUVIb3ZFcGJOQUJmZFVqZVpNT0Q4X25EemUxc0hObXlhYmpkelJFcVpRcDZIQVZRTjBVTzMyUW5iMXRTLVlqZW04ZjNNRmRKcTl6TUNHcnY2QjNDdUR5QzVBX2U3UjZySVdvUE83S2Q4ZkR3RzJfQ1lzUFFXUnc?oc=5) after the selloff, while [the big four hyperscalers are raising more than $131 billion in debt and equity for the buildout](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiygFBVV95cUxOdHdFY2V6VERyVE5OdGVxZ0xPWVE1UGRtc3NtdHRYVXlNdlRKQXNkQWU4dUhDNnhtMHFpVEU5T09fd0RXSHlFMkRIOHhZdF9MellSUHRYdUdmWHg0RFczRWZJbzFhb1dsb1B1X0J6YWJlQXE1RWZLMVBkVTFnSWRXRWdDd216NWVyQWxhaHBnakFUMnJBcDJEd3M1bHIzYkxIdVNkRndBZzZSMXdIeThkcHo1U2F4N2s2ellyZG1VZ2ZpWmszd3R5bVBB?oc=5) and [BofA flagged the boom as a major risk to the global economy](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiqAFBVV95cUxOSzdOdXV2TjY3ektTTHprX1hIMVlUNWI4Tl9VeERzNjlETEhRZ3JZcmhONXUtbDItVUVLVUZZNXdoZFplQk9NTVliWmFGeFFZWVdZaFB0dGw5UmU2UUVzTUE5UGVuSFh1Y1F2MEViWGlnNmNUYkpZX194YjhTOE9DdmpYaXMzZmNUWUc1Nm5Ob1NnMWVsNjBpbThqVDlmY3NBUWJjb2drZXU?oc=5). Chip shares [bounced back late in the week](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiW0FVX3lxTE5kNlQ2MXB3TldBa2dOdXBzUXpYUlNBenNaZTlFX3E1ZUE1V040UnpKQlVZSjNpWm1TVEx2NnRfWUowVmsydV85TEJHbjJKSVVUNTF1d1Y0YU5RYjQ?oc=5), and on Monday [chip stocks gained even as Nvidia said it was investigating a matter involving its chief executive](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMihgFBVV95cUxOMHF2UUhXOHRuenVSWGZ1NlNueXRTTlkzekE1UHNOVXNVeGNjUlh3QjFZUUx5bWdYRzFhT2t5cUc0b08teFF4R3RCVlMweEJuRGwxZVF3dm5VYVFpQTFERVpDeS1SZjFVcFpMRjMxYTVkUkNyQ2xVcWI5Q1FuaTA4RWVzUDFjUQ?oc=5), which the company's CEO addressed publicly ([WSJ](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMihwFBVV95cUxPSV9fWHdCZGw4OGdCbVpVMVJreGluVnp1TVhmT1JkemQ0RGdWQTZfNFNuODhETWJUQUt6NTVlUlRGY0NwNkRXOVd6VFlLSWFlTERpMEJWODJraHlyX3ZtRnFpSjUtVzhmOVVKNkRfS0RPZ3l4WHBnWEdwTTRRaVVDdmM3TEhxR0k?oc=5)). Reuters described the tone as [a fragile calm after AI whiplash](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMif0FVX3lxTE9fNFFqYzRzRm1EWVdXeFFaRUtfazI2a2dQVEFKVlVBcGt0S3pMN19wNmVuR1Vwal9yeHJQSFVYeU80SjdWc0hsM1V1ZDhGUjJZbDJ4Zlo3SVM0eHAxWEVTZGdFRHdRdnZsRTF2ZC1GM19ZTi1SWUYwZGtiSjkwTFE?oc=5).

## Company news and results

Earnings season rolled on away from the headlines. Kimberly-Clark reported third-quarter net sales of $4.1 billion in its SEC filing, down 0.4% on the prior year, with organic sales down 1.3%; adjusted gross margin of 35.5% was 130 basis points lower than a year earlier, and adjusted operating profit of $677 million was down 0.9%. Reported diluted EPS attributable to the company was $5.37 against $1.34 a year earlier, inflated by a roughly $1.4 billion pre-tax gain on a completed disposal; adjusted EPS on the same basis was $1.70, down 6.6%. The company said it completed its Kenvue transaction earlier in the week and reaffirmed its 2026 standalone outlook ([filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/55785/000162828026070514/kmbq32026ex-991.htm)). The detail that matters for the wider economy is in the margin commentary: unfavourable pricing net of cost inflation, offset by productivity savings — the same squeeze many consumer-facing firms describe. Elsewhere, [restaurant chains are refocusing on food quality to win diners back](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMifkFVX3lxTFA4b1docjM4TzdsZGN6MnBiRzA5R1Z4YWFWNUtxVC15bzRsV0VqbVFRZnNmM1AwLTlLN0hldUxMT0lBMzlabWowY0Fsallscl9PdXBpNTJ6STFRSGVlNlctQnJ4eDBzY0Jkd0lvRmV6VzA3cWllZ0h6WGg3d2FWdw?oc=5), another sign that price rises have reached their limit with consumers.

## Market mood

Nervous. The VIX at 23.42 on 9 November is up roughly 54% in a month, and CNN's Fear & Greed index reads 25 — "extreme fear" — against 44 a month ago, though slightly better than last week's 19. High-yield credit spreads, the extra yield investors demand to lend to riskier companies, widened to 3.48 percentage points on 5 November from 3.32 the previous day: a wobble, not a dislocation. Gold rose 4.17% on the week to $4,135 while bitcoin fell 7.29% and copper 3.38% — a classic defensive mix. Reddit's investing boards were dominated by chip and AI-linked tickers rather than broad index funds, which is unverified opinion but a useful gauge of where retail attention, and anxiety, is pointed. Futures pointed higher on Monday as [oil fell](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMid0FVX3lxTE5FVDc3UlZHcHBOWVJmWWs2YWxla3J5NkpsVmNlTERMM2lQNm1MdlRteDEyeUFGcGFKVHEzV0JGalFMZXlvV3o2R3dmb2dGWUh5WlpMOWxiYkdlb1c1RzB4WlNhQzRoTF9qM3lfaUlKeUhqQUFtWkdj?oc=5).
